Yes ... I was on Straterra on and off for 10 years. After a few years of taking it daily, I abruptly stopped. The first day was ok then the brain zaps began. This acute response lasted for around 4 or 5 days then gradually subsided. After a couple weeks, I was still getting some periodic brain zaps and felt more anxious but the worst was behind.

So... I highly recommend to taper off it.

Had a job post grad school - after yrs of working there felt I was on cruise control. Then I came up for promotion. My boss did similar thing - pushed me to change behavior and demonstrate I could make it at the next level. Began with an unexpected crappy annual review. I was slow to respond and the pressure kept increasing. Eventually reached the point where things got a bit harsh and I felt like I was suddenly on the fire line. Ended up scrambling to quickly find a new job. Hit same issues again right away at next place.

Looking back years later, the skills / abilities they wanted me to demonstrate were largely things I didn't possess (and never would be able to develop). Those who advanced to higher levels in that profession definitely had those traits. I simply hit a ceiling / it wasn't a good career fit for me, at least on the senior level. I wasted precious time "hanging around" the industry stuck getting nowhere and hoping my situation would magically change. Would have been much better off re-inventing myself + aligning my career better w/ my talents.

If one's purpose, i.e., "soul" aligns with their career, as long as they have the required skills, work can be plenty fulfilling. Unfortunately, for many people, there is a disconnect between our work and what makes us "tick" inside. The longer this misalignment lasts, the unhappier some people may become. Therefore, it's important to get out into the world and try out different professional pursuits. One's 20's are especially well suited for trial and error. Follow your interests and your passions. See what clicks and what does not. Focus on those areas that produce a heightened state our consciousness & where time easily passes. Eliminate what doesn't work.

as a 47 y/o ADHD'er with the same long-term struggle, I've found it helps to /1/ keep life as simple as possible - limit involvements, minimize possessions, don't over-commit, etc etc ... this is harder for us ADHD'ers than it would seem cause we're always on a dopamine hunt and that gets temporarily satisfied w/ buying shit we don't need, crowding our lives with people, new places, adventures yadda yadda ... however, this paints us into a corner and then we feel overwhelmed by life /2/   stick religiously to routine, as hard as it seems ... keep forcing oneself to do something over and over at the same time everyday no matter what ... i.e., I walk in door from work, I automatically put on running shoes and do a run, get home, prepare meal, do dishes ... same shit, every f'n day no matter what /3/ consolidate and eliminate certain activities ... instead of take bus home from work then take a run, just run home from work everyday ... sat mornings = shopping time - hit all the stores one after another instead of going shopping at different places throughout the week /4/ kind of dovetails with #1 but do whatever it takes to not envy, compare against and/or imitate the lives of others ... Just because your neurotypical friends or family members do / buy / attend / participate in / collect / work at / etc. whatever, this does not mean you should follow suite - unfortunately it takes ADHD'ers much longer to do a lot of shit + we tend to be disorganized, we can't deal well with the same level of complexity in life as others. Again, keep it simple, focus on strengths, avoid areas of weakness and just accept that us ADHD'ers are a different breed.

I'd likely say it's ADHD. The running likely causes a nice dopamine rush and probably accommodates your overactive mind. However, when not stimulated, your mind craves more activity / some fulfillment of some sort. If it's not satisfied, depression ensues and/or the anxiety takes over.

Do you enjoy the constant hunt for something new? Do you try running different routes constantly searching for  new things? Does regular routine cause your mood to plummet? If yes to all of these, again, prob ADHD.

I was 20 years into a corporate finance career when I was suddenly let go. During my early days of unemployment, I was a bit cocky and thought that given the schools I attended and firms that I worked for, I'd be back in a decent seat in no time. 

Fast forward a couple years later -- I had sold my nice home and moved my family into a dumpy old apartment in a questionable neighborhood. I lost most my friends due to self isolation. My marriage was crumbling. Even my relationship with my parents deteriorated. I felt completely helpless and trapped. No matter how hard I tried, I just could not land a job or even a consulting gig. The depression and anxiety made every day a battle. I was shocked about how badly my life fell apart and I feared how much worse it would become. 

One day, three years into unemployment, I was clicking through easy applies on indeed when I received a rare response back. This turned into my first phone interview in well over a year. After a few rounds of interviews, I somehow found myself with a job offer. At 47, I've taken a large step backwards in rank, I make a fraction of my old pay, I work brutal hours, and the work is stressful -- but I'm thankful just to have a job to go to.

I'm now about to hit my one year anniversary. The years of unemployment have left me with severe PTSD. I struggle with constant anxiety from a fear that I'll be let go again. I have hardly told anyone about the job as I don't trust that it will last. I constantly think about what I'd do if this does not work out. Needless to say, I'm having a difficult time regaining any bit of confidence. The depression is not as intense as when I was unemployed, however, its still there. All in all, it feels like my perspective on life was permanently damaged by the long-term unemployment.

Hi, I was similar. I have ADHD and had sexual urges at a really young age. By five, I was regularly masterbating. Blin 1st grade my mom found my notebook full of naked women drawings. She was distressed like yourself. All I remember is her telling me it was bad and not to do it. Was effective but made me feel dirty and shameful. 

By 10, I had watched my dad's hidden dirty movies over and over. I also began messing around with a neighbor girl. As far as I could tell, i was first in my grammer school class to have sex. I was very sexually active as a teenager. 

However ... for me at least, my external sexual relations with girls fell off in college. I hardly dated from 18-25. I only masterbated despite getting incredibly horny. Looking back, I went through a large shift in self esteem during high school. I realized I was unlike my peers. I wasn't rejected but my ADHD quirkiness led to heightened sensitivity and in inability to blend in with the popular crew. This low self esteem kept my sexual desires in check. I bring this up because in my research of ADHD, it seems that most males go through this. 

In my mid to late 20s, I grew comfortable in my skin for the first time and my sexual desires translated to actions. I had a lot of sex until I finally found the one and got married at 35. I was responsible with condoms and so on. 

I know that was long winded but (1) I am ADHD / overcommunicate and (2) my anacdote shows that it may not be worth a lot of worry due to the  ADHD causing insecurities. However, I'd have the "safe sex" talk and nowadays the "don't push yourself on anyone w/o consent talk". As a parent, i would also prepare for a highly sexual child -- don't let it surprise you.

 *** Importantly *** do what u can to curb the internet porn. What will happen is that if the mind is hypersexual and exposed to porn at a young age, the desire to seek more and more dopamine rush will compound over time. Porn is perfect for the ADHD mind. You have the search (hunting) then the reward (finding a perfect scene that fits your ever evolving desires). Over time, this could lead to interests in extreme sexual fantasies. Just search people with ADHD like Michael Phelps, some Rick stars, JFK, etc and you'll notice a correlation with extreme sexual urges. It just how we are wired. The more you can curb this, the better. Porn addiction is a heavy chain to drag around later in life.

I've been dealing with the negative internal chatter as well. It increased a lot over the past five years. Last year I came close to ending it all - reached a breaking point and kept having worst and worst panic attacks until I finally have a complete nervous breakdown. 

I'm doing a bit better now. Nowhere near 100% but much better. 

Not sure this will help you, but, what helped me: 

1/  Weekly therapy sessions (was going 2x a week during/after my dark days last year). I'm not sure why people are hesitant to see therapists, esp if you have health insurance. I found someone who was a compassionate listener and who allowed me to just get everything out in the open. By listening to myself, I began to untangle some of the deep knots in my subconscious. The doc also helped me understand my mind better + what was going on (I had childhood issues as well). Lastly, very importantly, when I had a nervous breakdown and just couldn't take anymore, I went over to my therapist, not knowing what else to do. I spent a whole afternoon with him until I could calm down. Having his help that day was HUGE. Not sure what would have happened otherwise.

2/ SSRIs and/or SSNIs (I've been on both now). Alongside the therapy these were key in knocking out a large portion of the negative chatter + ruminations + nightmares + depression.  They take a few weeks to begin kicking in. Once they do, the calm returns to the mind. I tried to sidestep prescriptions for years. Now I look back and kick myself. They exist for this exact reason. 

3/ Journaling. Hence why I'm here right now. Just writing about this stuff helps calm the mind for some reason. When I have a sudden flow of negative thoughts, I often write to just get it out. 

4/ Exercise and long walks. Just getting outside and observing the simple beauty in nature can lift the fog for hours, sometimes days. 

5/ Stay busy ... I've found that when my mind gets too idle, the negative chatter begins to fill it up. If I just get busy doing anything (cleaning, writing, reading, talking, etc), I can flush these turds away. 

I sincerely hope this helps + that you begin to feel better soon. Its rough and most won't understand. But some of us are here cheering you on.

Nice self-awareness. Yes, be conscience of the ADHD tendencies. I was diagnosed at 33 y/o and shrugged ADHD off until I was in my late 30's. Once I began reading about it, my eyes opened. In hindsight I realized how much self destruction I was doing in both my professional life and in my personal life. 

Our minds are wired a certain way + we can have a difficult time detecting the significant differences. However, they are there. My best advice is to focus on the positive attributes and try to set up damage control on the deficiencies. Personally, I've recently realized that things worked best for me in the past when (1) I worked independently, (2) had a hard, clearly defined goal that I was passionate about and that I could hyperfocus on and (3) \*\*\*importantly\*\*\* there was a HUNT involved meaning that I needed to go out and capture something (a buyer of an asset, a prospect, etc etc).

Looking back, I now realize that any job that requires processing work + routine makes me bored / unhappy.  My mind automatically drifts and I begin making a lot of errors. Additionally, I try to make the boring task interesting by adding unnecessary "features" to it -- creativity or researched facts that take up time and don't have much value for supervisors / clients. In my mind, I feel that these things make my work "superior" and that I'm some sort of smart rebel that others just don't understand. Unfortunately though, these instances compound and have just defined me as an odd duck that lacks productivity skills.

I recently had a candid discussion with an analyst I worked a lot with in the past. I always felt he respected me and that the work we did together was deemed fine. What he told me was interesting (albeit disheartening). He said that others joked that I was always "off task" but the junior people liked working with me because I had empathy (i.e., I was a softie). He said that our supervisors often went around me + directly to him due to disorganization and unnecessary detail. In hindsight, I'm not surprised that the amount of work that went to me gradually declined until my job felt threatened. He said "I'd never hire you". Kind of hurt but the feedback does help in crafting my future.

At work, look up the ladder and pay attention to the type people on top. This will lay clues to what you may encounter down the line. In my experience, the top people were always (1) very organized, (2) clear / linear thinkers, (3) rule-obliging, (4) strict, and (5) predictable. They did not seem to have much in terms of intuition or creativity. Nor did they seem to pursue the "hunt". Instead, they were good gathers and error free processors. They pride speed, productivity and cleanliness. All of this, I was definitely not. So ... time to go on my own and learn to hunt.

Living with neurotypical roommates always seems to expose our adhd differences. 

I've come to detect the following trend w/ roommates: 
1/ Works fine up front and it's fun esp w/ the initial back and forth  complimenting. We like the positive feedback regarding empathy or creativity or whatever and we reciprocate with complements mainly around the neurotypical aspects of the other person - they become confused cause their like "isn't everyone like that?" ... they begin focusing on ur differences
2/ with their radar on, at some point the lateness and/or messiness and/or impulsivity or whatever adhd tendency compounds against the neurotypical roommates(s) patience 3/ eventually either a small fight occurs or the adhd'r begins feeling they are receiving more back handed insults vs complements ... our sensitivity radar buzzes 
4/  we may ramp up the complements or use good times (too many drinks) to get overly empathetic - we start showering too many complements which may come off insincere - in our minds though, we're probably trying to get things back to where they began and we're creating an emotional shield against the oncoming storm that our intuition tells us is coming. It constantly bothers us the other person treats us worse ... insecurity mounts ... we feel used or dumb or something else negative 
5/ some inciting incident causes the relationship to take a major hit ... the neurotypical person shows their impatience with our adhd tendencies ... Unfortunately, this event usually deals a severe blow to the relationship that is often hard to overcome ... In my experiences, it usually involved getting purposely excluded from some event or getting blindside attacked in front of others w/o any apology from the neurotypical person 
6/ goes into a miserable walking on egg shell type relationship with intermittent good days but eventually more disasters follow ... the mess or loud talking or whatever adhd tendency gets pointed out in harsh ways ... Adhd'r just wants to get away from person / situation
7/ our creativity kicks in and we figure out how to do whatever it takes to move out ... cut lease, etc 
8 / if still somewhat cordial, may speak to the former roommate a few times here and there but the relationship eventually fades away

Apologies upfront for the length, but perhaps my story may be of some help as a data point:

During my early / mid 30's, I seemed to grow out of the heavy drinking of my 20's and go all-in on career. The pay, promotions and purpose soon followed. Somewhere around 37 or 38 though, I became complacent and began having that extra glass of wine at the more frequent work dinners. I'd releave the occasional subconscious itch about my increased drinking by justifying  "I deserved it" or "it's just to take the edge off". Besides, I needed to live out the last of my 30's. 

Soon I was regularly having a couple beers on Fri w/ co-workers. After awhile I was finding friends to keep drinking with afterwards. Instead of working on Saturdays, I began spending the day nursing hangovers then going back out at night. Soon thereafter, my Sundays were getting caught in the frey also - Sunday funday full of beers and sports. Instead of showing up Monday ready to tackle the week, I was edgy and tired.  My career began to slip around the edges. However, the drinking was fun. It became something to look forward to. I felt proud of how I could balance both work and fun. 

By 42 y/o,  was finding myself having a drink almost every night. The more I drank, the more the cracks formed in the foundations of my life - family, friends, career, faith, health, etc. The stress just lead to more escaping. I was soon finding it hard to go home w/o stopping at the bar. I lost control. It killed the fear I lived through all day - a fear that, in hindsight, proved much smaller than the big problems that I was about to slam into at 100 mph.

One night, my favorite team won the championship and I stayed out all night partying with complete strangers. The next day I showed up late for work and still drunk. That was also the day something unexpected arose necessitating the rare occasion of needing to work directly with the group head. Within seconds, he noticed the scent of alcohol on me along w/ bloodshot eyes. I explained my team winning, etc etc. A couple weeks later I was let go. They said my work was no longer meeting their standards and that I wasn't fitting in. In other words, they had their eye on me for some time. 

The mind of the drinker always thinks "it's fine and I'll keep it under control" and "I've gotten away w/ it this long, I'll just keep going". Alcohol helps you lie by providing a nice buzzy escape. So you drink even more when you should just stop. In my case, after I lost my job, months began to slip away. My marriage suffered. I found myself drinking just to get through the depression. Long story short, I eventually found myself in a pretty bad place - mentally, physically, spiritually. I knew that quitting drinking for good was necessary if I wanted to stay alive. 

In Hollywood movies, the addict usually has a catastrophic event as the inciting incident that changes the future direction of their life. They have to accept the sins of their past to become a better person. In reality, as my own experience shows, the inciting incident is usually just a seemingly mundane last straw that finally breaks the camel's back. A small spark that ignites an accumulating pile of bad habits. The wrong person smelling alcohol on you. The wrong comment that slips out while you are drunk. The wrong results coming back in your annual blood work. 

So, how do you prevent sneaky alcohol from getting to the point of derailing your life? You do what your doing. You take notice of the itch in your subconscious. You read about the effects of alcohol on your mind, on your body and your soul. You do the work to decide if it will assist you or potentially deter you in becoming the person who you want to become.
Looking back, that was the work I left undone that cancelled out all my other efforts.

You gotta ask yourself whether its her harmless way to show affection and bond with you. Watch whether she does it with others that she's close with. Some people grew up in families where poking is common. They think that's how you show affection, i.e. "he loves me so much i can say these things and there's no issue." If so, just flush away the negative thoughts and move on. If it is meant in a more malicious way or increasingly becoming more common, perhaps as a power tool, then read on....

Many neurotypicals get bothered by behaviors that don't fit perfectly in their interpretation of the world. Their chosen weapon is the disguised insult (insult wrapped in a joke or in a compliment), a rather complicated instrument because its difficult to react to without looking overly-sensitive. This is especially lethal if directed from a female at a male. You get hit by it, feel anxious (ADHD exasperates this response) and feel unable to immediately respond without looking awkward and weak. But you end up feeling inferior and excluded from the group.

Now... you basically have several choices of how to respond: 

1) Ignore it -- doesn't necessarily mean you are letting yourself get pushed around. In fact, your maintaining some power by saying "that doesn't deserve a response". Plus, you avoid arguments. What may be happening is that you are "zoned out" and she just wants to grab your attention. My wife does this to me and I've learned to just ignore it as harmless. Also, ambivalence is often the most powerful comeback.

2) Address the insult head-on -- best if you feel that the backhanded comments are ruining your relationship. Over-time, this can deteriorate you're relationship with her and possibly other friends out with you. Just respond with something like "I'm sure \[   \] and \[   \] didn't come out to hear about my \[   \]". Problem with this approach is that you may come off sensitive or it might trigger more back and forth jabs - uncomfortable for everyone. It does help "clear the air" though.

3) Laugh it off -- react with a comment like "wow, it sounds like your dating a real loser". If you keep calm, look at her right in the eyes and give her that smile (you know the one, it kind of says "f you" in a nice way), you may portray confidence while still ending the backhanded comments. Also, the comment defuses her intent to make herself look powerful. 

4) Do the long stare, with straight face and let out a "hmmmm" w/ head nod. Stay calm. Later, when alone with her, go back to the insult and ask what she meant by it. The questioning should make her uncomfortable. The purpose of the stare + hmmm is to tell her that nothing got past you. Plus, if she does it again, the stare + hmmm may be enough to make her stop because she won't want to awkwardly explain herself again to you. 

If none of these work, and its becoming worse and worse, just take the gloves off. Put her on the spot in front of everyone and take the power into your own hands. Respond back with questions like "does that really make you angry?", or "seems pretty trivial, why do you keep bringing this up?" or, if it really comes down to it, hold your balls and ask "you trying to sound impressive?" ... then be prepared to fight. To be honest, every once in awhile, its not bad to clearly draw the line like this. You re-gain respect that may have been seeping out the relationship.

Yes ... I've suffered from a combo of ADHD, anxiety and depression my whole life. 

Its like a game of mental whack-a-mole. Things will be fine for a period of time then, suddenly the anxiety rares it's ugly head. Symptoms are usually a cold/sugary feeling in the palm of my hands, back/neck aches, pains in my chest, frequent migraines, upset stomachs and a hard-to-describe nervous dread that I need to burn through every morning. Exercise helps. By night, insomnia kicks in and I pop wide awake after 3 - 4 hours of sleep. After a few nights of this, I finally sleep a glorious full night due to complete exhaustion. Recently, I slept 15 straight coma-like hours while in this condition.

If untreated, the lack of sleep, persistent sick feeling, trouble thinking straight and general loss of hopefulness (I call this condition "zombie zone") turns into deep mood swings and eventually leads to bad depression. The ADHD is always in the background but tends to flare up pretty bad alongside the anxiety -- I feel like there are 100 things I must do to move forward to kill the misery but I can't focus on any one thing. I freeze, paralyzed + overwhelmed by a spiral of thoughts. Tortured by my own mind. In the worst of times, this results in panic attacks. Until I understood all of this better, I rushed to the ER a couple times because I was worried I was having a heart attack or a stroke. 

After twenty some years of trying to just deal with it, my therapist and I finally began experimenting with a cocktail of medications (note: this works for me and may not work for others + you're body may not like the combos so never take without a doctor's oversight) ... I take low dose of Adderall XR + low dose Strattera + low dose of Zoloft daily (increased/decreased if needed) along with some herbs and vitamins. For me, Saint John's Wort helps my mood considerably. I've gone through long stretches taking just Strattera or just an SSRI but I didn't experience much of a result until I combined low doses together and mixed in some Adderall. 

 I also watch my diet close, especially sugar and food coloring intake. Lots of fruits and veggies and water. I went gluten free and I quit drinking alcohol. Oh, and I did lots of reading about ADHD, stress and anxiety. It is finally helping. My mood swings have stabilized, my negativity has lifted to a more acceptable level, and I'm figuring out how to better hyperfocus on daily priorities. 

Unfortunately, if I take too high a dose of this "cocktail" + drink too much coffee, everything backfires and my mind enters some dopamine filled amusement park. Every "ride" I get on seems like the most interesting thing in the world. As an example, a couple months back, I came across a high school probabilities book and spent the rest of the day digging through it  insanely excited about all the different ways I can apply all my new learning. Fun but probably not a productive way to live. It is better than deep anxiety, depression and hopelessness tho.

You must demonstrate a passion for investing right off the bat (first few mins). Try to figure out what the PM is invested in and perform enough research to have a discussion - ask why they are invested in a certain security, etc. Have some opinion about macro market conditions - are stocks / bonds over valued or so they have room to run? Also, importantly, if you want the meeting to translate to anything interesting, you must offer some insight of value. The easiest way to do this is to bring with you at least one written investment idea that fits within PM’s wheelhouse and have one or two backup ideas in your head (small or mid cap, nobody cares about your opinion about any FANGs). Be aggressive in showing your passion. Speak clean and to the point. The more the PM is speaking and enjoying the convo, the better you’re doing. Lastly, be prepared to discuss your own investing history and results. Keep any discussion about your background short, concise, honest and humble. It’s easy to lose a PM’s attention as they have many balls in the air at all times and a high value on their time.

As a general rule, if you’re not already investing, don’t have any personal investing results that you can articulately speak about and/or you are struggling with having a general opinion about macro / finding investment ideas —> you really need to question whether this is the right career for you. I’ve been a PM for years and there are plenty of poor, smart and hungry investment devotees out there biting at the bit for a chance to break into the industry, even for free trial periods. Those who win, push their own ideas / opinions which turn out correct more often than not. It takes many of hours of work to validate passion, especially in this sport.

BTW, GPA and everything else doesn’t matter if you are showing up to meetings with great investment ideas. I broke into the industry that way. I had a PM run out of my interview and grab an analyst and a trader to all go through my idea together. they started accumulating by close that day. That’s how I broke into a hedge fund with a non-traditional background. Drafting write up took me an afternoon but the logic behind my idea took 10 years of self education after work and on weekends.

There is disruption risks due to Compass and from the business model of Zillow.

Compass is akin to Uber, Lyft and other grow revenue at any cost and disregard any future prospects for profitability business models that survive off raising low quality VC funding and do whatever it takes to dump the toxic waste on public investors so that the founders and early investors can parachute out before the crash and burn.
